evidence: Verg. A. 9.658: ex oculīs ēvānuit (Lewis & Short)
Cic. de Or. 2.95: omnis eōrum memoria sēnsim obscūrāta est et ēvānuit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of things that fade until they are gone: a sound, a colour, a hope, a memory, a custom; with ex oculīs, of something seen. Lewis & Short also has it of wine that loses its strength with age (Cic. Div. 2.57).

terms.grammar: phrase; also sē ē cōnspectū auferre
evidence: Phaedr. App. 28.7–10: sēque ē cōnspectū abstulit
terms.comment: Of a person or an animal that goes off and is lost to view.

terms.grammar: phrase: nusquam with appāreō, verb, second conjugation
evidence: Ter. Eun. 4.3.18: ille bonus vir nusquam adparet (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The way to say that something is missing (keys, a shoe, a person): Latin says it appears nowhere.

phrases.latin: et procul in tenuem ex oculīs ēvānuit auram
phrases.english: and far off he vanished from sight into thin air

phrases.latin: vērum haec jam etiam inter ipsās ineptiās ēvānuērunt
phrases.english: but these (spellings) have now disappeared even among the follies

phrases.latin: vēnātor citus nōn intellēxit sēque ē cōnspectū abstulit
phrases.english: the hunter in his haste did not understand, and took himself off out of sight
that fine fellow is nowhere to be seen
